paper_title: RTAformer: Relation-Transition-Aware Transformer for Video Scene Graph Generation

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Video scene graph generation (VidSGG) aims to capture objects and their evolving relationships in videos. This requires accounting for both the persistence of object identities and abrupt changes in relationships. Existing methods aggregate information across frames to exploit temporal context, but an emphasis on consistency can obscure these changes. As a result, a model may retain its previous prediction even after the underlying relation has changed. We refer to this failure mode as relational semantic inertia. To address this issue, we propose Relation-Transition-Aware Transformer (RTAformer), a one-stage framework that separately models entity persistence and relation changes. It injects calibrated differences between adjacent-frame relation queries to guide predicate updates, while cross-frame instance alignment during training helps reduce cross-frame representational drift. Experiments on Action Genome show improvements in recall and mean recall over existing methods, with ablation studies supporting the contributions of the proposed components and comparisons using matched backbones showing larger gains on relation-transition frames than on non-transition frames.

Video scene graph generation (VidSGG) aims to capture objects and their evolving relationships in videos. Existing methods aggregate information across frames to exploit temporal context, but an emphasis on consistency can obscure these changes. As result, model may retain its previous prediction even after the underlying relation has changed. We refer to this failure mode as relational semantic inertia. To address this issue, we propose Relation-Transition-Aware Transformer (RTAformer), one-stage framework that separately models entity persistence and relation changes. It injects calibrated differences between adjacent-frame relation queries to guide predicate updates, while cross-frame instance alignment during training helps reduce cross-frame representational drift. sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Video scene graph generation (VidSGG) represents objects and their relationships in videos as structured subject, predicate, object triplets, with entities as nodes and relationships as edges. By explicitly representing who interacts with what and how these relationships evolve, video scene graphs provide structured information for action selection in embodied navigation and planning [9, 24, 34] and for interpreting events in video-language reasoning and question answering [3, 21, 27]. Approaches to VidSGG have evolved from multi-stage pipelines for object detection, temporal association, and relation classification [4,14,20] to one-stage frameworks that integrate instance and relation prediction, reducing reliance on external tracking [12, 29, 31]. Corresponding author. 2 J. Heo et al. Fig. 1: (a) Relational semantic inertia: the personcup/glass/bottle pair persists across frames, but its relation changes from looking at to not looking at, while the baseline [29] retains the previous predicate in the target frame. (b) Our reimplementation of the baseline exhibits an 11.6-point gap in SGDET R@10 between the non-transition and relation-transition frame subsets. Despite these advances, capturing abrupt relation changes remains challenging when the same entities persist across frames. While existing approaches aggregate information across frames to improve predictions [4, 8, 29, 31, 38], explicitly modeling relation changes for persistent entity pairs has received comparatively less attention. In such cases, model may retain its previous prediction even after the underlying relation has changed. Figure 1(a) illustrates this behavior: the same subjectobject pair remains visible, but its relation changes from looking at to not looking at, while baseline model [29] continues to predict looking at. Our reimplementation of the baseline [29] achieves an R@10 of 34.3 on the relation-transition frame subset, compared with 45.9 on the nontransition frame subset under the with constraint setting (Fig. 1(b)). We refer to this failure mode as relational semantic inertia. These observations motivate temporal modeling that preserves stable entity information while explicitly accounting for changes in relationships. To this end, we propose Relation-Transition-Aware Transformer (RTAformer), one-stage VidSGG framework that uses differences between adjacent-frame relation queries as explicit cues for predicate updates. RTAformer refines instance and relation queries in separate temporal streams to aggregate entity information and incorporate relation changes into predicate prediction. In the relation stream, adjacent-frame query differences are calibrated and injected before temporal aggregation. These differences are more informative when the queries remain grounded to consistent entity pairs across frames. We therefore regularize adjacent-frame instance-pair queries during training to encourage consistent grounding and help reduce representational drift in the transition cues. Our main contributions are as follows: 1. We characterize relational semantic inertia, failure mode in VidSGG where models retain previous predicate predictions despite relation changes between persistent entities. 2. We propose RTAformer, one-stage framework that separates entity and relation temporal refinement and uses calibrated relation-query differences RTAformer 3 as explicit cues for predicate updates, supported by cross-frame instance alignment that encourages consistent query grounding. 3. Experiments on Action Genome [11] demonstrate improved scene graph generation performance over state-of-the-art methods, with backbone-controlled comparison against OED [29] showing larger gains on the relation-transition frame subset than on the non-transition frame subset.

sections.title: 2 Related Work
sections.content: Video Scene Graph Generation. Video scene graph generation (VidSGG) extends image-based scene graph generation [5,10,13,25,33,35] by modeling objects and their relationships across video frames. Earlier methods typically separate object detection from subsequent temporal and relational reasoning [4, 26, 32], whereas recent one-stage frameworks integrate instance and relation prediction [12, 29, 31]. OED [29] and ARN [31] use learnable queries to predict instances and relations from visual features, while UNO [12] adopts an objectcentric slot-attention framework. Our work builds on the one-stage formulation by introducing explicit relation-change cues into temporal refinement. Temporal Aggregation and Relation Transitions. Temporal aggregation uses cross-frame context to refine instance and relation predictions. STTran [4] captures inter-frame dependencies with temporal transformer, APT [14] introduces anticipatory learning objectives, and DSG-DETR [8] uses object tracklets to exploit long-term dependencies. Within one-stage frameworks, OED [29] aggregates temporal information through cross-attention over instance and relation queries, while ARN [31] combines temporal feature modeling with entitypredicate association reasoning. Complementary efforts address prediction reliability, including memory-guided debiasing in TEMPURA [20] and selective spatio-temporal denoising in TD2-Net [15]. More directly related to our motivation, TR2 [30] addresses time-varying relations through text-guided supervision of inter-frame relation-feature differences. It also uses short-term message token to modulate the contribution of preceding-frame features during relation prediction. RTAformer shares the motivation of capturing relation changes but uses adjacent-frame differences as direct input to relation-query refinement. Specifically, it calibrates and injects these differences before temporal aggregation within one-stage framework, while separate instance and relation streams accommodate entity persistence and relation changes. Query-Based Temporal Modeling. DETR [1] formulates object detection as set prediction using learnable object queries, while subsequent methods incorporate explicit positional priors into query design [16,37]. For video understanding, queries also provide means of incorporating temporal information. FAQ [6] aggregates neighboring-frame evidence into queries for video object detection, while TrackFormer [18] and MOTR [36] propagate query states to maintain object tracks. In VidSGG, TPT [38] uses temporal propagation to connect predictions across frames. RTAformer focuses on differences between adjacent-frame relation 4 J. Heo et al. Because these differences can also reflect inconsistent entity-pair grounding, training-time instance alignment encourages cross-frame consistency to help reduce representational drift in the transition cues.

sections.content: RTAformer 5 ref , . . . , Nref As illustrated in Fig. 2, RTAformer is one-stage set-prediction framework that models the distinct temporal behaviors of entities and predicates in VidSGG. The framework consists of three key components. (1) Frame-Wise Spatial Triplet Parsing. Given target frame Itar and Nref reference frames {I 1 ref }, vision backbone [7, 23] followed by Transformer encoder [28] produces encoded visual features for each frame. These features are processed by two cascaded decoders, the Instance-Pair Decoder and the Relation Context Decoder, which transform Nq learnable triplet queries into frame-wise instance-pair queries Qins and relation queries Qrel. (2) Disentangled Temporal Aggregation (DTA). To mitigate relational semantic inertia, DTA refines the target queries Qins tar in separate instance and relation streams. The instance stream aggregates entity information across frames, while the relation stream applies Transition-Aware Delta Injection (TADI) to inject inter-frame relation-change cues into predicate decoding. (3) Spatio-Semantic Instance Alignment (SSIA). During training, SSIA applies contrastive regularization to adjacent-frame instance-pair queries to improve cross-frame query consistency and reduce representational drift in the displacements used by TADI. tar and Qrel

sections.title: 3.5 Spatio-Semantic Instance Alignment
sections.content: Because TADI computes displacement between same-index queries across adjacent frames, cross-frame query consistency is important for reducing representational drift in the displacement signal. Following prior work on same-index contrastive alignment for temporal representation learning [17], Spatio-Semantic Instance Alignment (SSIA) applies contrastive regularization to adjacent-frame instance-pair queries during spatial training. sections.title: 3.6 Optimization and Inference
sections.content: Set-prediction objective. We assign triplet queries to ground-truth annotations using Hungarian matching [1, 29], with weighted cost combining object and predicate classification with ℓ1 and GIoU terms for subject and object boxes. The training loss is LSGG = λobjLobj + λrelLrel + λL1Lbox L1 + λgiouLbox giou, (11) where λ denotes the loss weights. Object classification supervises all queries, with unmatched queries assigned to the no-object class. Predicate and box losses apply only to matched queries. The box losses supervise both subject and object boxes, while Lrel sums the classification losses for the attention, spatial, and contacting families. Decoupled optimization and one-stage inference. Following OED [29], we train RTAformer in two phases, first learning the spatial representations and then optimizing temporal refinement. In Phase 1, the spatial parser is trained with the backbone frozen, using frame-level supervision and SSIA regularization: Lstage1 = Lspatial SGG + λssiaLSSIA, (12) where Lspatial SGG denotes LSGG computed from the frame-wise spatial parsing outputs. In Phase 2, the backbone and spatial modules are frozen, and only the DTA module and temporal prediction heads are optimized on sequence-level clips: Lstage2 = Ltemporal (13) , SGG SGG where Ltemporal denotes LSGG computed from the temporally refined DTA outputs. This two-phase schedule is used only during training. At inference, RTAformer performs spatial triplet parsing, DTA, and final prediction without external trackers or temporal post-processing.

sections.title: 4 Experiments
sections.content: Dataset. Following prior VidSGG work [4, 14, 15, 20, 29, 31, 39], we evaluate our method on Action Genome (AG) [11], the standard benchmark for video scene graph generation. AG contains 234,253 annotated frames sampled from 9,848 videos, with 476,229 object bounding boxes and 1,715,568 relation annotations across 35 object categories excluding person and 25 predicate categories. The predicates are grouped into three semantic types: attention, spatial, and contacting. Evaluation Metrics. We evaluate our model under the standard scene graph detection (SGDET) protocol. SGDET requires the model to jointly localize object instances, classify their object categories, and predict the predicates between subjectobject pairs from video frames. We report recall@K (R@K) with {10, 20, 50} under two graph construction settings: With Constraint and No Constraint. The With Constraint setting restricts each subjectobject pair to its highest-scoring predicate prediction, whereas the No Constraint setting allows multiple predicate predictions for the same pair. Implementation Details. Our framework follows recent query-based one-stage VidSGG architectures [29, 31]. Following UNO [12], we use the same frozen DINOv2 vision transformer (ViT) backbone [7, 23]. The transformer encoder, instance-pair decoder, and relation decoder each contain six transformer layers, and the model uses Nq = 100 learnable triplet queries. In DTA, the instance and relation streams each contain three temporal aggregation decoders, each implemented as single transformer decoder layer. For SSIA, we set κ = 0.1, τ = 0.3, and λSSIA = 0.1. We train the model using the AdamW optimizer on four NVIDIA RTX A6000 GPUs. Unless otherwise specified, ablation studies use ViT-B/14, while the main comparisons report ViT-S/14, ViT-B/14, and ViT-L/14 variants. Additional implementation details are provided in the supplementary material.

sections.title: 4.2 Ablation Studies
sections.content: Effect of SSIA and DTA. Table 2 reports module-level contributions. Both SSIA and DTA improve over the spatial baseline, and their combination achieves the highest recall across all evaluated cutoffs and settings. SSIA remains beneficial when DTA is enabled, increasing R@10 from 41.2 to 42.2 under with constraint. Effect of Transition-Aware Delta Injection. Table 3 compares transition cue injection designs within the relation stream. Temporal aggregation without injection already improves over the spatial+SSIA baseline, supporting the benefit of temporal context. Injecting relation-query displacement further improves performance, with raw delta consistently outperforming direction-only injection. TADI achieves the highest recall across all evaluated cutoffs and settings, supporting the effectiveness of the complete calibrated injection design.

(5) over the 105,356 persistent pair adjacencies. As rq increases across equal-count deciles, transition prevalence rises monotonically from 20.9% to 55.4%, compared with the overall rate of 33.7% (Fig. 4(b)). sections.title: 5 Limitations
sections.content: Although SSIA improves same-index temporal consistency and qualitative observations suggest that same-index queries can maintain consistent subjectobject grounding across adjacent frames, DETR-style decoding does not guarantee exact cross-frame query correspondence. Our evaluation is limited to Action Genome under the SGDET setting, and broader evaluation across VidSGG datasets and protocols would strengthen evidence for generalization.

sections.title: 6 Conclusion
sections.content: Reliable video scene graph generation requires models to recognize when previously valid relation no longer describes the observed interaction. We examine this challenge through relational semantic inertia, drawing attention to outdated predicate predictions that persist even as relationships between visible entities change. RTAformer uses calibrated relation-query changes to guide predicate updates, and experiments on Action Genome show improved SGDET performance, with backbone-controlled comparison revealing larger gains on relationtransition frames than on non-transition frames. Our analyses connect these performance observations with evidence that relation-query displacement carries information about predicate transitions. Together, the characterization of this failure mode and the transition-focused evaluation provide concrete basis for future work to examine responsiveness to relation changes alongside overall prediction accuracy.

sections.title: Alignment
sections.content: We first clarify the index correspondence used throughout this analysis. RTAformer represents each candidate interaction by triplet query indexed by {1, . . . , Nq}. At frame t, the instance-pair query Qins t,q predicts the subject and object of the q-th candidate, while the relation query Qrel t,q predicts the predicate for the same candidate pair. This correspondence follows from the cascaded decoding design: Qrel is produced by applying the Relation Context Decoder to Qins , with no sorting, reassignment, or re-indexing between the instance-pair and relation stages. Therefore, the predictions at index are combined to form the q-th triplet subject, predicate, objectq. During training, Hungarian matching supervises the subject, object, and predicate predictions at the assigned query index as single triplet, using joint cost over object classification, predicate classification, and box localization. Thus, within each frame, index defines one triplet candidate shared by the instance-pair and relation predictions. SSIA is designed to stabilize this index-level instance-pair grounding across adjacent frames. This property is important for RTAformer because TADI computes same-index relation-query displacements between adjacent frames. If the same-index queries were not grounded to consistent subjectobject pairs, the resulting displacement could reflect representational drift rather than genuine relation transition. Therefore, this section provides additional analysis showing that SSIA induces temporally consistent instance-pair query representations. S2.

sections.title: Illustration of SSIA Validity Masking
sections.content: Before analyzing the trained query representations, we first illustrate the validity masking used in SSIA. SSIA does not force every same-index candidate pair (Qins ) constructed from GT-matched target query to be close. Int,qm stead, candidate pair is used as positive anchor only when the target-frame object matched to query qm has same-category object with sufficient spatial , Qins t1,qm RTAformer: Supplementary Material 5 overlap in the previous frame. Otherwise, the pair is masked out from the SSIA contrastive objective. This masking prevents SSIA from incorrectly pulling together query embeddings when the corresponding object-side entity is not verified to persist across adjacent annotated frames. Thus, SSIA encourages temporal consistency only for reliable cross-frame anchors, rather than imposing same-index alignment unconditionally. Fig. S1: Example of SSIA validity masking. The target frame contains an annotated cup/glass/bottle, while the corresponding object is not annotated in the previous frame. Therefore, the same-index pair (Qins t1,qm ) fails the spatio-semantic validity check and is not used as positive anchor in the SSIA loss. t,qm , Qins S2.2 Representation-Space Visualization of Same-Index Query

sections.title: Consistency
sections.content: Using the same spatio-semantic persistence criterion for sample selection, we qualitatively examine the representation space of same-index instance-pair queries. We visualize instance-pair query representations extracted from the Action Genome test split using t-SNE. We compare two spatial parsers trained with the same configuration, with and without SSIA. For both variants, we collect GT-matched and class-consistent cross-frame pairs whose bounding boxes satisfy IoU > 0.3 across adjacent annotated frames. We then select the 15 most represented query slots and randomly sample 60 temporal pairs per slot, yielding 900 temporal instance pairs per model. For each variant, embeddings from frame and frame 1 are projected into shared two-dimensional t-SNE space. As shown in Fig. S2, SSIA produces more organized query representation space. Same-index query embeddings from adjacent frames remain closer to each other, whereas the model trained without SSIA shows more dispersed embeddings and longer cross-frame links. This supports the role of SSIA as training-time regularizer that reduces instance-level representation drift before relation-query displacement is used by TADI. 6 Fig. S2: t-SNE visualization of cross-frame instance-pair query representations. Circles and triangles denote embeddings from frame and frame 1, respectively, and colors indicate query slot indices. line segment connects the same-index temporal query pair (Qins t1,q). With SSIA, same-slot embeddings form more compact clusters with shorter cross-frame segments, indicating improved temporal consistency of instance-pair query anchors. Without SSIA, same-slot embeddings are more dispersed and connected by longer, crossing segments, suggesting stronger cross-frame representational drift. t,q , Qins S2.3 Temporal Grounding Consistency of Same-Index Queries We next examine whether the representation-space alignment in Fig. S2 has corresponding image-space effect. We use the SSIA-trained frame-wise spatial parser from Phase 1, before applying DTA, and run it independently on four consecutive annotated frames from each clip. No reference frame, temporal aggregation, tracking, IoU matching, or other cross-frame association is used. Thus, boxes with the same color in Fig. S3 are direct frame-wise predictions from the same query index. Following the person-centric annotations of Action Genome, we omit person boxes and visualize only object-side predictions for clarity. Since the subject side is the person in these visualized examples, object-side consistency corresponds to stable personobject candidate grounding. Fig. S3 shows that the visualized same-index queries maintain object-side grounding across annotated frames under purely frame-wise inference. In the first clip, the same query indices consistently localize the sandwich and dish despite hand motion and object displacement. In the second clip, they remain grounded to clothes and the floor region across the frame sequence. This qualitative check complements Fig. S2 and supports the role of SSIA in stabilizing instance-pair query anchors before TADI computes same-index relation-query displacements.
